rule/seq: A model reads the letters K, D, R, A, M, and then K again. What comes next?
rule/guess: The letters are random, so no rule of English helps. But the text itself does: the last time K appeared, D came right after it. So guess D.
rule/repeat: Real text repeats like this all the time. A story names Nora Quill, and the next time Nora comes up, Quill is the best guess, though nothing but the text says so.
rule/induction: Guessing a rule from examples is called induction: K was followed by D before, so expect D after K again. Induction heads are named for it.
rule/history: In 2021, Nelson Elhage, Chris Olah and colleagues, in the paper that named the residual stream, found small transformers doing this with two attention heads in different blocks, or layers.
rule/two: It only ever appeared in models with at least two layers. Why does it take two?
prev/need: To predict D, a head at the second K must find the D. Its query can only match keys, and each key is made from its own position's stream.
prev/blind: At first, the D's stream holds only D. Nothing in it says that a K came just before.
prev/back: So in a lower layer, a previous-token head attends one position back, at every position.
prev/write: It writes what it finds into the stream. Now position one, the D, carries a note: my previous token was K.
prev/order: Writes stay, so every layer above can read the note. The same layer cannot: its heads all read the stream before any of them writes.
match/query: In a higher layer, at the second K, the induction head's query asks for a key that says: my previous token was K.
match/hit: Only position one's key says that, so the head attends there, to the D. The causal mask allows it: the D is in the past.
match/copy: Its value carries D, so the head copies D into the second K's stream.
match/score: So when the model scores the next token, D's score goes up: seen K D, now K, predict D.
match/pair: Neither head does this alone. Together, they continue any pattern the text has already shown, whatever the letters are.
match/olsson: In 2022, Catherine Olsson and colleagues saw induction heads form suddenly, early in training, in models of every size they studied, as long as the model had more than one layer.
